reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Brenner and Rector's The Kidney
clinicalPearls: Caused by deposition of calcium oxalate crystals within the tubules and interstitium, producing acute or chronic kidney injury
Biopsy shows polarisable, birefringent, often fan-shaped calcium oxalate crystals in tubular lumina with surrounding tubular injury and interstitial inflammation
Secondary (enteric) hyperoxaluria from fat malabsorption is a common cause, notably after bariatric surgery, in inflammatory bowel disease or pancreatic insufficiency
Other causes include primary hyperoxaluria (inherited hepatic enzyme defects), excessive dietary oxalate or vitamin C, and ethylene glycol poisoning
Presentation ranges from unexplained acute kidney injury to progressive chronic kidney disease, sometimes with nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis
Enteric hyperoxaluria arises because unabsorbed fatty acids bind calcium, leaving free oxalate to be absorbed in the colon

Management addresses the cause: drug withdrawal and supportive care in toxin-related cases, dietary oxalate restriction and calcium supplementation with bile-acid handling in enteric disease, and specific therapy for primary hyperoxaluria
reference.pathophysiology: Oxalate is an end-product of metabolism that is renally excreted, and when plasma and tubular oxalate rise, calcium oxalate supersaturates and precipitates as crystals within the tubular lumina. These birefringent crystals obstruct and directly injure tubular epithelial cells, triggering inflammasome activation, interstitial inflammation and fibrosis, which drive acute kidney injury and, with sustained exposure, progressive chronic damage and nephrocalcinosis. Hyperoxaluria may be primary, from inherited defects of hepatic glyoxylate metabolism causing endogenous overproduction, or secondary, from enhanced enteric absorption in fat malabsorption, high oxalate or ascorbic-acid intake, or acute overproduction as in ethylene glycol poisoning. Declining renal function further impairs oxalate clearance, creating a self-amplifying cycle of systemic oxalate accumulation.
additionalDifferentials: Acute tubular injury or acute interstitial nephritis of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Renal biopsy with polarised microscopy demonstrating birefringent calcium oxalate crystals
24-hour urinary oxalate excretion and plasma oxalate
Assessment for fat malabsorption and relevant gastrointestinal or bariatric history
Genetic testing for primary hyperoxaluria in appropriate cases
Dietary and supplement history including vitamin C intake
Renal imaging for nephrocalcinosis and stones
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or dialysis-requiring acute kidney injury with widespread crystal deposition
Systemic oxalosis with extrarenal crystal deposition in advanced disease
Suspected ethylene glycol poisoning with metabolic acidosis and an osmolar gap
Recurrent nephrolithiasis with declining renal function suggesting primary hyperoxaluria
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the cause and the crystal and fibrosis burden at diagnosis; reversible or treatable causes may allow partial renal recovery, whereas heavy crystal deposition with interstitial fibrosis and untreated ongoing hyperoxaluria often progresses to end-stage kidney disease. Primary hyperoxaluria carries a particularly poor renal prognosis without disease-specific treatment, and dialysis alone poorly clears oxalate.
pitfalls: Overlooking oxalate nephropathy as a cause of unexplained acute kidney injury
Failing to take a bariatric-surgery, malabsorption or supplement history
Missing primary hyperoxaluria in patients with recurrent stones and early renal failure
Not recognising ethylene glycol poisoning as an acute cause
Assuming standard dialysis adequately clears the systemic oxalate load
management: Treat the underlying cause: manage enteric hyperoxaluria by correcting fat malabsorption, and in ethylene glycol poisoning give fomepizole and haemodialysis to halt oxalate generation

Reduce oxalate burden with a low-oxalate diet, oral calcium taken with meals to bind intestinal oxalate, restriction of vitamin C, and a bile-acid sequestrant such as cholestyramine in fat malabsorption
In primary hyperoxaluria use high fluid intake, pyridoxine in responsive type 1 disease, oral citrate to inhibit crystallisation, and RNA-interference therapy such as lumasiran
Maintain generous hydration to reduce tubular calcium-oxalate supersaturation
Provide renal replacement therapy for severe acute kidney injury and manage progression toward chronic kidney disease
Monitor urinary and plasma oxalate, renal function, and nephrocalcinosis or stone burden on imaging
Refer to nephrology, consider combined liver-kidney transplantation for primary hyperoxaluria with advanced kidney failure, and offer genetic counselling in inherited disease
